title: Pinnacle Airlines 3701

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Crash of Pinnacle Airlines Flight 3701, Bombardier CL-600-2B19, N8396A, Jefferson City, Missouri, October 14, 2004

location.name: Residential area about 2.5 miles south of Jefferson City Memorial Airport, Missouri

summary: On a night repositioning flight with no passengers, the two pilots flew the CRJ-200 in an unprofessional manner, including a pitch-up manoeuvre and a climb to the aircraft's 41,000 ft ceiling at a low airspeed. The aircraft stalled at FL410, both engines flamed out during the upset, and the engine cores subsequently seized (core lock). The crew did not restore power or reach an airport and the aircraft crashed in a residential area near Jefferson City, killing both pilots.
probable_cause: The NTSB determined the probable cause was (1) the pilots' unprofessional behavior, deviation from standard operating procedures, and poor airmanship, which resulted in an in-flight emergency from which they were unable to recover, in part because of the pilots' inadequate training; (2) the pilots' failure to prepare for an emergency landing in a timely manner, including communicating with air traffic controllers immediately after the emergency about the loss of both engines and the availability of landing sites; and (3) the pilots' improper management of the double engine failure checklist, which allowed the engine cores to stop rotating and resulted in the core lock engine condition. Contributing were the core lock engine condition, which prevented at least one engine from being restarted, and the airplane flight manuals that did not communicate to pilots the importance of maintaining a minimum airspeed to keep the engine cores rotating.

factors.evidence: The pilots performed a pitch-up manoeuvre, exchanged seats in flight and climbed to FL410 at a low airspeed in vertical speed mode contrary to standard operating procedures.
The crew allowed airspeed to decay during the climb and at FL410 without recognising the approaching stall.
The stick shaker and then the stick pusher activated at FL410 as the aircraft approached and entered the stall.
The aircraft stalled at FL410 and the resulting upset disrupted airflow to both engines.
The pilots pulled against the stick pusher rather than reducing pitch attitude to recover.
Both engines flamed out during the stall and neither could be restarted; the aircraft crashed after a power-off glide.
The NTSB cited the pilots' inadequate training in high-altitude aerodynamics and stall recovery as part of the probable cause.
The crew initially told ATC only one engine had failed and did not promptly communicate the double engine failure or prepare for a forced landing.
The airplane flight manuals did not communicate the importance of maintaining a minimum airspeed to keep the engine cores rotating after a flameout.
The double engine failure checklist did not adequately guide pilots to maintain windmilling airspeed before attempting restarts.
The forced landing attempt was made at night with no power in a residential area.

events.text: Repositioning flight departs Little Rock for Minneapolis with only the two pilots on board.
Shortly after takeoff the crew performs an abrupt pitch-up manoeuvre reaching about 1.8 g.
The pilots exchange seats during the climb.
Crew decides to climb to FL410, the aircraft's maximum certificated altitude ('forty-one it'), and request the level from ATC.
Climb continued in autopilot vertical speed mode at about 500 ft/min; airspeed decays progressively as the aircraft approaches FL410.
Aircraft levels at FL410 at a low airspeed; the autopilot holds altitude while the airspeed continues to decrease.
Stick shaker activates; the autopilot disconnects.
Stick pusher activates repeatedly; the pilots pull back against the pusher and the aircraft stalls.
Both engines flame out during the upset; the aircraft is now without engine power.
Crew declares an emergency to ATC but reports the loss of only one engine.
Crew attempts windmill restarts but keeps the airspeed well below the 300 kt required by the checklist, so the engine cores do not spin up.
APU started at lower altitude; APU-assisted restart attempts fail as the engine cores have seized (core lock).
Crew finally informs ATC that both engines have failed; ATC provides vectors toward Jefferson City Memorial Airport.
Controller gives distance and heading to the airport; the crew reports they will not make the runway.
Crew remarks they are going to hit houses as the aircraft descends in darkness toward a residential area.
Aircraft strikes trees and the ground in a residential area about 2.5 miles south of the airport; both pilots are killed, no one on the ground is injured.

recommendations.text: Require CRJ operators and the manufacturer to revise flight manuals and checklists to state the minimum airspeed needed to keep engine cores rotating after a double engine failure and to address the core lock condition.
Require air carriers to provide training in high-altitude aerodynamics, stall recognition and stall recovery at high altitude, including the correct response to stick pusher activation.
Address unprofessional behaviour and non-adherence to standard operating procedures on non-revenue repositioning flights through operator oversight and pilot professionalism programs.

safety_changes: Bombardier revised CRJ flight manuals and the double engine failure checklist to emphasise maintaining airspeed to keep the engine cores rotating and to describe core lock.
Airlines added high-altitude aerodynamics and stall recovery training, and the accident became a standard case study in pilot professionalism.

notes: t0 is set to the approximate time of stick shaker activation at FL410 (about 21:54 CDT); event times other than takeoff (21:21), flameout (about 21:55) and impact (about 22:15) are approximations to the nearest few minutes.
Flight number, MSN and coordinates are approximate; coordinates mark the general crash area south of Jefferson City.
Recommendation numbers were not recalled with confidence and are left null.
No CVR quotations included; the widely reported 'forty-one it' remark is paraphrased as a crew_speech event.
